cards.narration: Pia likes stickers. She counts them in groups of ten. Here are 10 stickers. That is 1 ten.
Pia keeps counting. Ten tens make one hundred. A hundred is a big group.
Now Pia has 1 hundred, 2 tens, and 4 ones. We read it as one hundred twenty-four.
We can break 124 apart. It is 100 and 24. The amount stays the same.
Here is another way. 124 is 12 tens and 4 ones. Ten tens are 100, and 2 more tens make 12.
Here are 4 ones. Add them to 12 tens. You get 124 again.
Great job, Pia! Now you can read and build numbers to 200. Let's practise!
Meet Mia the frog. Mia loves to collect shells. Today she wants to learn which number is greater.
Mia has 12 shells. Her friend Sam has 8 shells. 12 is greater than 8. 8 is less than 12.
Now Mia has 125 shells. Sam has 152 shells. Both numbers have 1 hundred. So Mia checks the tens next.
125 has 2 tens. 152 has 5 tens. 2 tens is less than 5 tens. So 125 is less than 152.
Mia can also use a benchmark. 85 is less than 100. 130 is greater than 100. So 130 is greater than 85.
Now put numbers in order. Least to greatest means smallest first. The numbers 48, 95, and 130 are in that order.
Greatest to least means biggest first. That order is 130, then 95, then 48. Now let's practise with Mia!
Mia has 6 cookies. She shares them with 1 friend. That is 2 children. Each child gets the same.
Now Mia has 4 chocolate bars. She shares them with 3 friends. Each friend gets 1 bar.
One bar is left over. Mia cuts it into 3 equal parts. Each friend gets one part.
So each friend gets 1 whole bar and one third of a bar. That is 1 and one third.
Next, 5 pies are shared by 2 friends. Each gets 2 pies. One pie is left. Cut it in halves. Each gets 2 and one half.
Share whole things first. Cut what is left into equal parts. Now you try!
Mia has one yummy pizza. She wants to share it fairly with her family.
First, Mia cuts the pizza into 3 equal slices. One slice is one third of the pizza.
Next, Mia cuts another pizza of the same size into 6 equal slices. One slice is one sixth.
Now Mia takes 2 slices of the sixths. That is two sixths of the pizza.
Look! Two sixths is the same amount as one third. The slices are different, but the amount is equal.
Two thirds is the same amount as four sixths too. Smaller slices means you take more of them.
You found that one third equals two sixths. Now let's practise with Mia!
Mia has 5 apples. 3 are red and 2 are green.
Swap the numbers. 2 + 3 is also 5. Adding in any order gives the same answer.
Mia has 4 apples. She adds 0 more. Zero changes nothing. She still has 4.
Now Mia has 9 apples. She gives away 4. Now 5 are left.
Let's check. Add the 4 back to the 5. We get 9 again. It matches!
Frog hops 2, then 2, then 2. That is three equal jumps. It lands on 6.
Now you try. Use order, zero, checking, and equal jumps!
Meet Jo. Jo has 8 apples in a basket. Then Jo picks 8 more apples.
8 and 8 is a double. Doubles are easy to know. 8 + 8 = 16. Jo has 16 apples.
Now 9 + 4. Take 1 from the 4 and give it to the 9. That makes 10. Then 10 + 3 = 13.
Try 7 + 8. Use a double. 7 + 7 = 14. Then add 1 more. 7 + 8 = 15.
Take away is adding in reverse. What is 13 - 9? Think 9 + 4 = 13. So 13 - 9 = 4.
Jo knows doubles, making 10, and think addition. Now it is your turn to practise!
Meet Mia. She is a baker. She puts 4 cookies on a plate.
Now she fills 3 plates. Each plate has 4 cookies. That is 3 groups of 4.
Add the groups to count them all. 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. Mia has 12 cookies.
Next, Mia cuts a pizza into 4 equal slices. Each slice is one fourth.
4 groups of one fourth make 1 whole pizza.
A sandwich is cut into 2 halves. 6 groups of one half make 3 whole sandwiches.
Great job! Equal groups add up fast. Let's practise!
Mia has 8 cookies. She wants to share them with her friends.
Mia has 2 plates. She shares the cookies equally. Each plate gets the same number.
One for this plate, one for that plate. Again and again. Each plate gets 4 cookies.
Now Mia has 12 muffins. She puts 3 muffins in each bag. How many bags can she fill?
Count by 3s. 3, 6, 9, 12. That makes 4 bags.
Division can find how many in each group. It can also find how many groups.
You know how to share equally now. Let's practise!

items.narration: Pia has 1 hundred, 4 tens, and 2 ones. What number is that?
items.why: 1 hundred is 100. 4 tens is 40. 2 ones is 2. Put them together to get 142.

items.narration: How many tens make one hundred? Is it 5, 10, 20, or 100?
items.why: Ten tens make one hundred. Count by tens ten times to reach 100.

items.narration: Move the frog to 150.
items.why: 150 is halfway between 100 and 200. Count by tens from 100: 110, 120, 130, 140, 150.

items.narration: Which number is one hundred twenty-six? Is it 162, 126, or 106?
items.why: One hundred twenty-six is 1 hundred, 2 tens, and 6 ones. That is 126.

items.narration: What is 100 + 7?
items.why: There are no tens. So 1 hundred and 7 ones is 107.

items.narration: Sam has 150 beads. How many tens is that?
items.why: 10 tens make 100. 5 more tens make 50. So 150 is 15 tens.

items.narration: 124 is 100 and how many more? Is it 24, 42, 4, or 12?
items.why: Take away the 100 from 124. What is left is 24.

items.narration: Move the frog to 165.
items.why: 165 is 1 hundred, 6 tens, and 5 ones. Go to 160, then 5 more.

items.narration: 12 tens and 5 ones is the same as 152. Is that true or false?
items.why: 12 tens is 120. Add 5 ones to get 125, not 152. So it is false.

items.narration: A box holds 10 pencils. Sam has 14 boxes. How many pencils is that?
items.why: 14 tens is 10 tens and 4 tens. That is 100 and 40, so 140.

items.narration: Mia has 9 tens and 15 ones. What number is that?
items.why: 9 tens is 90. 15 ones is 10 and 5. So 90 and 10 make 100, and 5 more is 105.

items.narration: Which number is the same as 17 tens and 6 ones? Is it 167, 176, or 76?
items.why: 17 tens is 170. Add 6 ones to get 176.

items.narration: Move the frog to the number with 17 tens and 5 ones.
items.why: 17 tens is 170. Add 5 ones to land on 175.

items.narration: 164 is 1 hundred, 5 tens, and how many ones?
items.why: 100 and 50 make 150. From 150 to 164 is 14 more. So there are 14 ones.

items.narration: Which is greatest, 1 hundred 9 tens, 18 tens 5 ones, or 17 tens 9 ones?
items.why: 1 hundred 9 tens is 190. 18 tens 5 ones is 185. 17 tens 9 ones is 179. So 190 is greatest.

items.narration: Which number is greater, 87 or 120?
items.why: 120 has 1 hundred. 87 has no hundreds. So 120 is greater than 87.

items.narration: Which number is less, 150 or 105?
items.why: Both have 1 hundred. 105 has 0 tens and 150 has 5 tens. So 105 is less.

items.narration: Is 190 closer to 100 or closer to 200?
items.why: 190 is only 10 away from 200. It is 90 away from 100. So it is closer to 200.

items.narration: Which number is greater, 94 or 149? Type the greater number.
items.why: 149 has 1 hundred. 94 has none. So 149 is the greater number.

items.narration: Move the frog to 100.
items.why: 100 is halfway between 0 and 200. Count the jumps of 50 to find it.

items.narration: Which number is the greatest, 138, 183, or 118?
items.why: All have 1 hundred. Now check the tens. 8 tens is more than 3 tens or 1 ten. So 183 is greatest.

items.narration: Mia puts 150, 105, and 115 in order from least to greatest. Which number goes first?
items.why: Least to greatest starts with the smallest. 105 has the fewest tens. So 105 goes first.

items.narration: Here are 163, 136, and 183. Type the least number.
items.why: All have 1 hundred. 136 has 3 tens. The others have more tens. So 136 is least.

items.narration: Put 120, 87, and 150 in order from least to greatest. Type the middle number.
items.why: The order is 87, then 120, then 150. The middle number is 120.

items.narration: Here are 140, 90, and 120. Move the frog to the least number.
items.why: 90 has no hundreds. 140 and 120 each have 1 hundred. So 90 is the least.

items.narration: True or false? 99 is greater than 101.
items.why: 101 has 1 hundred. 99 has none. So 101 is greater, and the sentence is false.

items.narration: Here are 175, 157, 171, and 177. Type the greatest number.
items.why: All have 1 hundred and 7 or 5 tens. Compare the ones in 175, 171, and 177. 177 is greatest.

items.narration: Type the number that is greater than 168 and less than 170.
items.why: Count up from 168. The next number is 169. Then comes 170. So 169 is between them.

items.narration: Here are 165, 156, and 175. Move the frog to the greatest number.
items.why: All have 1 hundred. 175 has 7 tens. The others have 6 tens or 5 tens. So 175 is greatest.

items.narration: Here are 60, 180, and 120. Move the frog to the middle number when they go from least to greatest.
items.why: The order is 60, then 120, then 180. The middle number is 120.

items.narration: 6 cookies are shared by 2 friends. How many cookies does each friend get? Is it 2, 4, 3, or 6?
items.why: Give each friend one cookie at a time. After 3 rounds, all 6 cookies are gone. Each friend gets 3.

items.narration: 8 apples are shared by 4 friends. How many apples does each friend get?
items.why: Hand out 1 apple to each of the 4 friends. Do it again. That uses all 8. Each gets 2.

items.narration: 10 stickers are shared by 2 friends. Drag the frog to how many stickers each friend gets.
items.why: Split the 10 stickers into 2 equal groups. Each group has 5 stickers.

items.narration: 4 bars are shared by 3 friends. Each gets 1 bar. One bar is left. Into how many equal parts do we cut it? Is it 2, 3, 4, or 6?
items.prompt: Cut the left bar into how many parts?
items.why: There are 3 friends. So the left bar is cut into 3 equal parts. Each friend gets one part.

items.narration: 9 pears are shared by 3 friends. How many pears does each friend get?
items.why: Make 3 equal groups from 9 pears. Each group has 3 pears.

items.narration: 4 sandwiches are shared by 3 friends. How much does each friend get? Is it 1 1/3, 1 1/2, 2, or 1 2/3?
items.why: Each friend gets 1 whole sandwich. One is left. Cut it in 3 parts. Each friend gets 1 and one third.

items.narration: 7 crackers are shared by 3 friends. How many whole crackers does each friend get? Drag the frog to the number.
items.why: Each friend gets 2 crackers. That uses 6. One cracker is left to cut up.

items.narration: One pie is cut into 4 equal parts. 4 friends share it. What part does each friend get? Is it 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, or 2/3?
items.why: The pie has 4 equal parts for 4 friends. Each friend gets 1 part. That is 1/4.

items.narration: 5 cookies are shared by 2 friends. How much does each friend get? Is it 2, 2 1/2, 3, or 2 1/4?
items.why: Each friend gets 2 whole cookies. One is left. Cut it in halves. Each friend gets 2 and one half.

items.narration: 10 bars are shared by 3 friends. Each friend gets 3 whole bars. How many bars are left over?
items.why: 3 friends each get 3 bars. That is 9 bars. 10 take away 9 leaves 1 bar.

items.narration: 2 bars are shared by 3 friends. Each bar is cut into 3 equal parts. How much does each friend get? Is it 1/3, 1/2, 2/3, or 2?
items.why: Cut each bar into thirds. Each friend takes one third from each bar. That is 2 thirds.

items.narration: Some bars were shared by 3 friends. Each friend got 3 and one third bars. How many bars were there?
items.why: 3 friends each got 3 whole bars. That is 9 bars. The 3 thirds make 1 more bar. 9 + 1 = 10.

items.narration: 10 bars can be shared by 3 friends or by 6 friends. Who gets more each? 3 friends or 6 friends?
items.why: With fewer friends, each share is bigger. 10 bars shared by 3 friends gives more than by 6 friends.

items.narration: 10 granola bars are shared by 3 friends. How much does each friend get? Is it 3, 3 2/3, 5, or 3 1/3?
items.why: Each friend gets 3 whole bars. That uses 9. One bar is left. Cut it in thirds. Each gets 3 and one third.

items.narration: 10 bars are shared by 6 friends. Each friend gets 1 whole bar first. How many bars are left? Drag the frog to the number.
items.why: 6 friends each get 1 bar. That uses 6 bars. 10 take away 6 leaves 4 bars to cut up.

items.narration: A pizza is cut into 3 equal slices. One slice is picked. What fraction is picked? Is it 1/6, 1/2, or 1/3?
items.why: The pizza has 3 equal slices and 1 is picked. So one third is picked.

items.narration: Mia cuts a pizza into sixths. That means equal slices. How many slices does the pizza have?
items.why: Sixths means 6 equal slices. You can count them in the picture too. There are 6.

items.narration: Three thirds make one whole pizza. A pizza is cut into thirds. How many slices make the whole pizza?
items.why: Thirds means 3 equal slices. All 3 slices make the whole pizza.

items.narration: Which picture shows one third of a pizza? Is it 1 of 6 parts picked, 1 of 3 parts picked, or 1 of 2 parts picked?
items.why: One third means 1 of 3 equal slices. The pizza cut into 3 slices with 1 picked shows it.

items.narration: A pizza is cut into 6 equal slices. Two of the 6 slices are picked. How many sixths are picked?
items.why: Two slices are picked. Each slice is one sixth, so two sixths are picked.

items.narration: Leo eats one third of a pizza. Which is the same amount of that pizza? Is it 1/6, 3/6, or 2/6?
items.why: Cut each third into 2 sixths. One third is 2 sixths.

items.narration: One third of a pizza equals how many sixths of that pizza?
items.why: Each third can be cut into 2 sixths. So one third equals 2 sixths.

items.narration: Two thirds of a pizza equals how many sixths of it?
items.why: Each third is 2 sixths. Two thirds is 2 and 2 more, which is 4 sixths.

items.narration: Is one sixth of a pizza equal to one third of it? Yes or no?
items.why: One sixth is a small slice. One third is bigger. Two sixths would equal one third.

items.narration: Two sixths of this pizza are picked. Cut the same pizza into 3 equal slices instead. How many thirds are picked?
items.why: Two sixths is the same amount as one third. So 1 slice is picked.

items.narration: This strip has 4 sixths picked. Which fraction is the same amount? Is it 1/3, 1/2, or 2/3?
items.why: Every 2 sixths make 1 third. So 4 sixths make 2 thirds.

items.narration: Ben ate 4 sixths of a pan of brownies. That is the same as how many thirds of the pan?
items.why: Two sixths make one third. Four sixths make two groups, so 2 thirds.

items.narration: Three friends each eat one third of a pizza. The pizza is cut in sixths. How many sixths do they eat all together?
items.why: Each friend eats 2 sixths. Three friends eat 3 times 2, which is 6 sixths.

items.narration: Mia ate 2/6 of a pizza. Leo ate 1/3 of the same pizza. Who ate more? Mia ate more, Leo ate more, or same amount?
items.why: Two sixths is the same as one third. So they ate the same amount.

items.narration: A pizza is cut into 6 equal slices. Zoe eats one third of the pizza. How many sixths are left?
items.why: One third is 2 sixths. Take 2 slices from 6 and 4 are left.

items.narration: You know 5 + 3 = 8. What is 3 + 5? Is it 5, 3, 8, or 9?
items.why: Adding in any order gives the same answer. 5 + 3 and 3 + 5 are both 8.

items.narration: What is 6 + 0?
items.why: Adding zero changes nothing. 6 plus 0 is still 6.

items.narration: Move the frog to the answer of 4 + 3.
items.why: Start at 4 and hop 3 more. 4, 5, 6, 7. The answer is 7.

items.narration: Frog hops 2, then 2, then 2. How far did it go in all? Is it 6, 5, 4, or 8?
items.why: Add the equal jumps. 2 and 2 is 4. Then 4 and 2 is 6.

items.narration: What is 8 - 0?
items.why: Taking away zero changes nothing. 8 take away 0 is still 8.

items.narration: Is 8 + 6 the same as 6 + 8? Yes or no?
items.why: Adding in any order gives the same answer. Both 8 + 6 and 6 + 8 make 14.

items.narration: You know 12 - 5 = 7. Add to check. What is 7 + 5?
items.why: Adding back what you took away gets you to the start. 7 + 5 is 12.

items.narration: Move the frog to the answer of 15 - 0.
items.why: Taking away zero changes nothing. So 15 - 0 is 15.

items.narration: We know 14 - 6 = 8. Which sentence checks it? Is it 8 + 6 = 14, 8 + 8 = 16, 14 + 6 = 20, or 6 + 6 = 12?
items.why: To check, add the answer to the part you took away. 8 + 6 makes 14.

items.narration: Sam hops 5, then 5, then 5. How far did he go in all?
items.why: Add the equal jumps. 5 and 5 is 10. Then 10 and 5 is 15.

items.narration: Ben gave away 8 stickers. He has 9 left. How many did he have at the start?
items.why: Add the stickers back to check. 9 left plus 8 given away is 17.

items.narration: Mia adds 6 + 9 + 4. What is the total? Is it 18, 19, 20, or 21?
items.why: Add in any order. Make a ten first: 6 + 4 is 10. Then 10 + 9 is 19.

items.narration: Frog starts at 0 and jumps by 5, four times. Move the frog to where it lands.
items.why: Count the jumps: 5, 10, 15, 20. Four jumps of 5 land on 20.

items.narration: Which is the same as 4 + 4 + 4? Is it 3 jumps of 4, 3 jumps of 3, 4 jumps of 4, or 2 jumps of 4?
items.why: 4 + 4 + 4 has three equal groups of 4. That is 3 jumps of 4, which makes 12.

items.narration: Lia found that 25 - 9 = 16. Add to check it. What is 16 + 9?
items.why: Add the answer to the part taken away. 16 + 9 is 25, so Lia is right.

items.narration: What is 5 + 5? Is it 8, 10, or 12?
items.why: 5 and 5 is a double. Count 5, then 5 more. You get 10.

items.narration: Jo has 6 stars. Jo gets 3 more stars. How many stars now?
items.why: Start at 6. Count up 3 more: 7, 8, 9. The answer is 9.

items.narration: Move the frog to the answer of 4 + 5.
items.why: Start at 4 and hop 5 times. You land on 9.

items.narration: What is 10 - 4? Is it 5, 6, or 7?
There are 9 birds. 5 birds fly away. How many birds are left?
What is 8 + 8? Is it 14, 18, or 16?
items.why: 8 and 8 is a double. Double 8 is 16.

items.narration: What is 9 + 5? Make 10 first.
items.why: Take 1 from 5 to make 9 into 10. Then 10 + 4 = 14.

items.narration: Move the frog to the answer of 12 - 5.
What is 14 - 6? Is it 7, 8, 9, or 10?
items.why: Go back to 10 first. 14 - 4 = 10. Then take away 2 more to get 8.

items.narration: What is 7 + 8? Use a double to help.
items.why: 7 + 7 = 14. Then add 1 more. The answer is 15.

items.narration: 8 + 9 = 17. Which take-away fact goes with it? Is it 17 - 9 = 8, 17 - 8 = 8, or 17 - 7 = 9?
items.why: Take one part away from 17 to get the other part. 17 - 9 = 8.

items.narration: 8 plus what number makes 15? Find the missing number.
items.why: Count up from 8 to 10. That is 2. Then 5 more to reach 15. 2 + 5 = 7.

items.narration: Move the frog to the answer of 16 - 7.
Which sum is greatest? Is it 7 + 7, 6 + 9, or 8 + 6?
Sam has 20 stickers. Sam gives away 12 stickers. How many stickers are left?
items.why: Think 12 + 8 = 20. So Sam has 8 stickers left.

items.narration: Here are 4 ducks. Each duck has 2 legs. How many legs in all?
items.why: Add 2 four times. 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8. So there are 8 legs.

items.narration: Mia has 3 groups of 4 cookies. Which adds up to 3 groups of 4? Is it 3 + 4, 4 + 4, or 4 + 4 + 4?
items.why: 3 groups of 4 means you add 4 three times. That is 4 + 4 + 4.

items.narration: Frog hops 2 at a time. It makes 3 hops from 0. Move the frog to where it lands.
items.why: Hop 2, then 4, then 6. 2 + 2 + 2 = 6.

items.narration: Here are 3 hands. Each hand has 5 fingers. How many fingers in all?
items.why: Add 5 three times. 5 + 5 + 5 = 15. So there are 15 fingers.

items.narration: A pizza is cut into 4 equal slices. Each slice is one fourth. How many fourths make 1 whole pizza? Is it 4, 8, or 2?
items.why: The pizza has 4 equal slices. All 4 fourths together make 1 whole pizza.

items.narration: Leo has 6 bags. Each bag has 3 apples. How many apples in all?
items.why: Add 3 six times. 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 18. Leo has 18 apples.

items.narration: Frog hops 5 at a time. It makes 7 hops from 0. Move the frog to where it lands.
items.why: Count by 5s seven times. 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35. The frog lands on 35.

items.narration: A tricycle has 3 wheels. There are 4 tricycles. How many wheels in all? Is it 7, 12, or 9?
items.why: Add 3 four times. 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12. There are 12 wheels.

items.narration: Here are 2 pizzas. Each pizza is cut into 4 equal slices. Eight slices are picked. That is 8 groups of one fourth. How many whole pizzas is that?
items.why: Every 4 fourths make 1 whole pizza. 8 fourths is 2 groups of 4. So it is 2 wholes.

items.narration: Ben has 4 feet. Each foot has 5 toes. How many toes in all? Is it 9, 15, 20, or 25?
items.why: Add 5 four times. 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20. Ben has 20 toes.

items.narration: Frog hops one half at a time. It makes 8 hops from 0. Move the frog to where it lands.
items.why: Two hops of one half make 1. Eight hops make 4 groups of 2 hops, so the frog lands on 4.

items.narration: A half carton holds 6 eggs. Sam has 7 half cartons. How many eggs in all?
items.why: Add 6 seven times. 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 42. Sam has 42 eggs.

items.narration: Which makes the most? Is it 5 groups of 2, 3 groups of 5, or 4 groups of 3?
items.why: 5 groups of 2 is 10. 3 groups of 5 is 15. 4 groups of 3 is 12. So 15 is the most.

items.narration: Here are 3 pizzas. Each pizza is cut into 4 equal slices. Every slice is one fourth. How many fourths in all?
items.why: Each pizza has 4 fourths. Add 4 three times. 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 fourths.

items.narration: Frog hops 4 at a time. It makes 8 hops from 0. Move the frog to where it lands.
items.why: Count by 4s eight times. 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32. The frog lands on 32.

items.narration: Mia shares 6 apples equally between 2 friends. How many apples does each friend get? Is it 2, 3, or 4?
items.why: Give one apple to each friend again and again. Each friend gets 3 apples.

items.narration: Ben has 10 cookies. He shares them equally on 2 plates. How many cookies are on each plate?
items.why: Share the cookies one at a time to each plate. Each plate gets 5 cookies.

items.narration: Eight stickers are shared equally by 4 friends. Move the frog to how many stickers each friend gets.
items.why: Share 8 stickers with 4 friends, one at a time. Each friend gets 2 stickers.

items.narration: Sam has 6 fish. He puts 2 fish in each bowl. How many bowls does he fill?
items.why: Count by 2s. 2, 4, 6. That is 3 bowls.

items.narration: Zoe has 4 balloons. She shares them equally between 2 kids. How many balloons does each kid get? Is it 1, 3, or 2?
items.why: Give one balloon to each kid, then one more to each. Each kid gets 2 balloons.

items.narration: Pat has 12 peaches. He packs them equally in 3 baskets. How many peaches are in each basket? Is it 3, 4, 5, or 6?
items.why: Share the peaches one at a time into 3 baskets. Each basket gets 4 peaches.

items.narration: Pat has 12 peaches. He puts 4 peaches in each basket. How many baskets does he fill?
items.why: Count by 4s. 4, 8, 12. That is 3 baskets.

items.narration: Nine grapes are shared equally by 3 kids. Move the frog to how many grapes each kid gets.
items.why: Share 9 grapes one at a time with 3 kids. Each kid gets 3 grapes.

items.narration: Ella has 12 cookies. She shares them equally with 6 friends. How many cookies does each friend get?
items.why: Give each of the 6 friends one cookie. Then give each friend one more. Each gets 2.

items.narration: Ava has 10 beads. She puts 5 beads in each bag. How many bags does she fill? Is it 3, 5, or 2?
items.why: Count by 5s. 5, 10. That makes 2 bags.

items.narration: Nia has 12 cookies. Who gets more cookies each: 2 friends sharing the 12, or 4 friends sharing the 12? Is it 2 friends or 4 friends?
items.why: 12 ÷ 2 = 6, but 12 ÷ 4 = 3. Fewer friends means bigger shares.

items.narration: Leo has 12 stars. He puts 2 stars in each group. How many groups does he make?
items.why: Count by 2s up to 12. 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. That is 6 groups.

items.narration: Twelve muffins go into bags. Each bag holds 4 muffins. Move the frog to how many bags Mia fills.
items.why: Count by 4s. 4, 8, 12. That is 3 bags.

items.narration: We know 4 groups of 3 make 12. Now share 12 things equally into 4 groups. How many are in each group?
items.why: 4 groups of 3 make 12. So 12 shared into 4 groups gives 3 each.

items.narration: Kim has 9 plums. She gives 3 plums to each friend. How many friends get plums? Is it 3, 2, or 4?
items.why: Count by 3s. 3, 6, 9. That is 3 friends.
